## Stage check
Architecture context (access rules and trust boundaries) is present inline. Code is present. All 14 items will be reviewed.

---

## 14-Item Security Checklist

**1. SECRETS — OK** (`/.env`, `checkout/index.ts`, `stripe-webhook/index.ts`)
`VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY` is in the browser bundle, but the anon key is Supabase's intended public credential; every table is gated by Row Level Security (RLS — database-level rules that decide who can see or change each row). The three genuinely dangerous secrets (`STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`, `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`) are in Supabase's server-side secrets store and never appear in committed files.

**2. DATABASE ACCESS — ISSUE** (`001_init.sql`)
All four tables (`user_roles`, `services`, `bookings`, `messages`) have RLS enabled with correct policies. However, the storage `SELECT` policy for `client-files` contains no ownership check — flagged in full under item 11.

**3. AUTHORIZATION — OK** (`checkout/index.ts`, `stripe-webhook/index.ts`)
`checkout` verifies the user's JWT (JSON Web Token — a signed login credential) before doing anything, then looks up the price itself instead of trusting the browser. `stripe-webhook` verifies Stripe's cryptographic signature before trusting the event. File-write authorization is enforced server-side (own-folder check in the SQL policy). The file-read gap is the item 11 issue.

**4. INPUT — ISSUE** (`src/pages/Files.jsx`)
File type and size checks (`ALLOWED`, `5_000_000`) are browser-only. Any attacker can call the Supabase Storage API directly and upload an executable or a 500 MB file; JavaScript in the browser is never a real barrier. `Messages.jsx` is safe: React automatically escapes text so it can't be injected as HTML. The 2 000-character body limit is a database constraint, which is server-enforced. The file check is not.

**5. PAYMENTS — OK** (`checkout/index.ts`, `stripe-webhook/index.ts`)
Price is read from the database by the server, not sent by the browser. The webhook calls `constructEventAsync` with the shared secret before touching any data — meaning a forged webhook from a random attacker is rejected. The `upsert` with `onConflict: 'stripe_session'` prevents a race condition from booking the same session twice.

**6. AI / LLM — NOT APPLICABLE**
No AI or large-language-model features in the codebase.

**7. RATE LIMITS & ABUSE — ISSUE** (`supabase/functions/checkout/index.ts`)
There is no per-user rate limit on the checkout Edge Function (a serverless function that runs on Supabase's infrastructure). A logged-in user can fire it hundreds of times a minute, generating hundreds of Stripe Checkout sessions at no marginal cost to them but real cost to you.

**One-sentence pitch:**

1. **Your parents will tap the app reliably every day.**
This is the whole bet. Two people in their late 70s–early 80s need to open an app on the right screen at the right time, every single day, without help. *Cheap test:* set up a WhatsApp group poll ("Did you take your 8am meds? Yes / No") for one week and count how many days both parents actually respond. If that fails, the app fails too.

2. **A missed or delayed tap won't be read as a missed dose — with a blood thinner involved.**
Real-time sync (the technical term for multiple devices seeing the same data the instant it changes) can fail silently: bad Wi-Fi, the app crashing, an accidental double-tap. If your sister sees "not taken" and calls your dad to retake a blood thinner he already took, that's a medical emergency. *Cheap test:* write down every way the status could show wrong, and decide right now whether a disclaimer is enough or whether you need a confirmation step.

3. **You can build and host something reliable enough for this use case inside $20/month.**
Lovable (a no-code app builder) paired with Supabase (a free-tier backend — think of it as a live database that syncs data between all four phones) can handle four users easily. # ARCHITECTURE.md

## 1. Stack Decision

*A few terms used in this table:*
- **Serverless function** — code that runs on demand when called, with no server you manage or pay for when idle.
- **Row Level Security (RLS)** — rules baked into the database itself that control who can read or change each row, enforced on the server side.
- **Hosted checkout** — the payment page lives on the payment provider's servers; card data never touches your code.

| Layer | Choice | Why | Rejected alternative & why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Frontend** | React (TypeScript), generated and hosted by Lovable | Lovable decides this — it generates React apps | — |
| **Backend / API** | Supabase Edge Functions (Deno serverless) | Lives in the same Supabase project as the database; no separate server to manage; Lovable integrates with Supabase natively | Separate Express.js server on Render — requires terminal to deploy and maintain |
| **Database** | Supabase PostgreSQL with RLS | Comes built into Supabase; relational structure (an order must belong to a real slot) matches the spec; RLS lets the database itself enforce who can see what, server-side | Firebase Firestore — looser data structure, harder to enforce atomic slot counts and server-only price rules |
| **Auth** | Supabase Auth (Owner only); server-issued signed session token (Helper); UUID order token in URL (Customer) | Three roles need three different trust levels; one real login, one PIN session, one anonymous private link | Auth0 / Clerk — cost money at scale; more than needed for a one-owner app |
| **File storage** | None in V1 | No image uploads in scope | Supabase Storage — can add in V2 for menu photos |
| **Payments** | Square Hosted Checkout | Spec requires Square; hosted checkout means card data never touches your code or server | Stripe — spec requires Square |
| **AI / LLM** | None | Not in spec | — |
| **Hosting** | Lovable (frontend CDN) + Supabase (backend, database, edge functions) | Both have usable free tiers; Lovable already hosts what it builds | Vercel + separate DB host — more accounts, more configuration |
| **SMS / Notifications** | Twilio | Simplest SMS API; well-documented; free trial credit to start (~$0.008/SMS after that) | AWS SNS — more complex setup; email-only — spec says SMS |

> **Budget note:** Hosting is $0/month on free tiers. Square charges a per-transaction percentage (no monthly fee). Twilio charges per SMS (~$0.008) plus ~$1.15/month for a US phone number — unavoidable for SMS delivery. Trial credit covers all your initial testing.

## 4. Trust Boundaries

### What runs in the browser (untrusted)

The browser — including every line of JavaScript Lovable generates — is untrusted. Anyone can open browser developer tools and inspect everything there.

The browser **may**:
- Display public data fetched from the database (menu items, slot times, computed availability)
- Show the customer their own order status via `order_token` in the URL
- Show the helper the masked queue after receiving a valid session token from the server
- Redirect the customer to the Square checkout URL

The browser must **never** hold:
- Square API keys
- Twilio keys
- The raw `helper_pin_hash`
- Any customer phone number (except the owner's own view, which arrives masked from the server)
- Price calculations or slot-count calculations — these must come from the server

---

### What runs on the server (Edge Functions — trusted)

Every one of these operations must live in an Edge Function, never in a React component:

| Operation | Why it must be server-side |
|---|---|
| Calculate order total | Spec requires server-only totals; a customer could fake a lower price if the browser calculated it |
| Check slot availability and create a hold | Must be an atomic database transaction; the browser cannot be trusted to count correctly |
| Create Square checkout session | Requires the Square API key |
| Verify Square payment webhook | Requires checking Square's webhook signature |
| Mark order as paid | Only after confirmed payment signal from Square |
| Verify Helper PIN and issue session token | PIN hash must never leave the server |
| Return queue to Helper with masked phone | Raw phone never leaves the server; masking happens here |
| Send SMS via Twilio | Requires Twilio credentials |

---

### Where roles are stored and how they are enforced

| Role | Where stored | Can the user edit it? |
|---|---|---|
| Owner | Supabase Auth user table; RLS policies check `auth.uid()` against a fixed owner record | No — set only via the Supabase dashboard; not in any user-editable profile field |
| Helper | Nowhere permanently — role is asserted by a short-lived JWT (*a signed ticket*) issued by the Edge Function after a correct PIN, stored in the browser only as a cookie the server sets | No — the token is signed with a server secret; the browser cannot forge or alter it |
| Customer | No account — role is implied by possessing a valid `order_token` UUID | No — the token is a random UUID created by the server; the customer cannot create or modify one |

### ⚠️ Lovable risk flag

Lovable sometimes generates Supabase client calls directly in the frontend for operations that should be Edge Functions. The **anon key** (the public key embedded in the frontend) is safe to expose — but RLS must block everything it shouldn't reach. Specifically, Lovable may generate code that:

- Reads `customer_phone` directly from the Orders table in the browser → must be blocked by RLS
- Reads `helper_pin_hash` from Settings → must be blocked by RLS
- Creates Order rows directly from the frontend → must be rejected by RLS; use an Edge Function instead
- Calls the Square API from the browser → must **never** happen; the Square key lives only in Edge Function secrets

**After every Lovable build session:** review any generated file containing `supabase.from('orders')`, `supabase.from('settings')`, or the word `square`. If it is inside a React component or hook instead of an Edge Function, move it before going live.

| **Supabase** | Database, auth, edge functions, backend hosting | Service Role Key (admin) + anon key (public) | Service Role Key → Edge Function env only; anon key → embedded in frontend (safe, RLS enforces access) | 500 MB database; 50,000 monthly active authenticated users; 500,000 Edge Function calls/month; 5 GB bandwidth | Whole app is down; nothing to do but wait; monitor at status.supabase.com |
| **Lovable** | Frontend hosting + code generation | n/a — OAuth to your Lovable account | n/a | Free tier available — check current limits at lovable.dev/pricing | Frontend is unreachable; database and orders are intact; re-deploy resolves it |

| Item | 0 orders | 100 orders/month | 1,000 orders/month |

| **Total platform cost** | **$0** | **~$2/month** | **~$9/month** |

Square fees come out of your sales revenue, not a separate invoice.

---

## 7. Decisions Log

**These are final unless you explicitly change them.**

- **ADR-1:** Use Supabase PostgreSQL because relational structure with enforced relationships matches slot/order/item data and RLS provides server-side access control without extra code.
- **ADR-2:** Use Supabase Edge Functions for all sensitive operations because they run in the same project as the database, require no separate server, and hold secret keys away from the browser.
- **ADR-3:** Use Square Hosted Checkout (not Square Elements/SDK) because the spec requires Square and hosted checkout means card data never touches our server or code.
- **ADR-4:** All order totals are calculated server-side in an Edge Function by reading current prices from the database; any price the client sends is ignored.
- **ADR-5:** Slot availability is computed server-side inside an atomic database transaction to prevent overbooking; available count is never a client-writable or client-trusted field.
- **ADR-6:** 5-minute holds are implemented as a `hold_expires_at` timestamp on the Order row; expired holds are released lazily (filtered out at the moment the next booking attempt checks availability) to avoid needing a background job on the free tier.
- **ADR-7:** Customer phone numbers are stored only in the database; the raw phone is returned only to the authenticated Owner; the Helper receives a masked version (e.g., ●●●-●●●-1234) computed by the Edge Function before the response is sent.
- **ADR-8:** The Helper PIN is stored only as a bcrypt hash in the Settings table; the hash is never returned in any response; the Edge Function compares the submitted PIN against the hash server-side and issues a signed session token if correct.
- **ADR-9:** Customer `order_token` is a random UUID generated server-side; it is unpredictable and is the sole credential a customer uses to view their own order status.
- **ADR-10:** Supabase Auth is used only for the Owner; no Supabase Auth account is created for Helpers or Customers, keeping auth complexity and free-tier user counts minimal.

---

## 8. Known Risks

**Risk 1: Lovable generates client-side code for sensitive operations**
Lovable's AI may write code that calls Square or reads phone numbers from the frontend directly.
*Mitigation:* After every generation session, search for `supabase.from('orders')`, `supabase.from('settings')`, and `square` in generated files. If found in a React component, move that logic to an Edge Function before going live.

**Risk 2: Concurrent bookings cause overbooking**
Two customers clicking "Book" at the same millisecond could both pass the availability check.
*Mitigation:* The Edge Function that creates a hold must wrap the availability check and order creation in a single PostgreSQL transaction with a row-level lock (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) on the Slot row, so only one request proceeds at a time.

**Risk 3: Square webhook not delivered**
If Square can't reach your Edge Function URL (brief outage, misconfigured URL), the order stays in "held" and the customer has paid but isn't in the Helper queue.
*Mitigation:* Store the `square_checkout_id` on every order. Add a manual "re-check payment" button on the Owner dashboard that queries Square's API by checkout ID. Log all incoming webhooks so you can replay them.

**Risk 4: Expired holds build up**
If customers abandon checkout, their holds linger until the next booking attempt cleans them up lazily.
*Mitigation:* Lazy cleanup (filter `hold_expires_at > NOW()` on every availability check) is sufficient for low-volume V1. The UI can show a note: "Slots free up automatically if checkout is abandoned." Upgrade to a scheduled cleanup job if volume grows.

**Risk 5: Twilio trial credit runs out mid-service with no warning**
The $15.50 trial credit disappears silently and ready SMS stops sending.
*Mitigation:* Add a real payment method to Twilio before going live (the actual per-SMS cost is tiny). Add error logging so the Owner dashboard surfaces SMS failures. The app still works — the helper just needs to call orders by name until it's fixed.

---

## 9. In Plain English

- **Your app has three layers:** a public website (what everyone sees in their browser), a set of behind-the-scenes functions that do the sensitive work (counting slots, talking to Square, masking phone numbers), and a locked database. You never touch a server directly — the platforms run it all.

- **Square handles every dollar.** When a customer pays, they leave your site and land on Square's page. Square tells your app "payment confirmed" automatically. Your code never sees a card number, ever.

- **Phone numbers never leave the back room.** The helper's screen shows something like ●●●-●●●-1234. Only you, as the owner, can see the full number. It never appears in a web address, a download, or a helper's browser.

- **The 5-minute hold works like a parking meter.** When a customer starts checkout, a timer starts in the database. If they don't pay in 5 minutes, the slot opens up automatically for the next person — no action required from you or the helper.

- **The "free" part is real for hosting, but SMS costs pennies.** You pay nothing monthly for the website and database at this scale. Twilio charges less than one cent per text message. Square takes a small cut of each sale, which comes out of the sale itself rather than a separate bill.

---

## 10. Accounts to Set Up Before Building

- [ ] **Lovable** — lovable.dev — Free tier. Sign up to get your workspace and check current free-tier limits at lovable.dev/pricing before building.

- [ ] **Supabase** — supabase.com — Free tier. Create a new project (takes about 2 minutes to provision). Note your project URL and anon key — Lovable will need them to connect.

- [ ] **Square Developer Account** — developer.squareup.com — Free. You need:
  - A Square *merchant* account (free to create)
  - A *Developer Application* inside the developer dashboard
  - Your **Access Token** and **Location ID** from the dashboard
  - A webhook endpoint URL (you'll get this from your deployed Supabase Edge Function URL)
  - ⚠️ Allow 1–2 days to test in Square's sandbox (practice mode) before switching to live payments.

- [ ] **Twilio** — twilio.com — Free trial (~$15.50 credit). You need:
  - A Twilio account (email verification only, fast)
  - A US phone number provisioned in the Twilio console (~$1.15/month after trial)
  - Your **Account SID** and **Auth Token** from the console dashboard
  - ⚠️ **Critical for US SMS — plan for 3–7 business days:** Businesses texting US mobile numbers must register under a carrier compliance program called **A2P 10DLC** (*Application-to-Person 10-Digit Long Code* — it just means "a verified business texting from a normal phone number"). Twilio guides you through this registration inside their console. Without it, US carriers will silently block or filter your messages. **Start this registration the same day you create your Twilio account.** It is the only step in this whole project that takes more than a few minutes to approve.

---

## Context Carry

**Platform:** Web only (no app store).

**Stack:** React frontend (Lovable CDN) → Supabase Edge Functions (all sensitive logic) → Supabase PostgreSQL with RLS + Supabase Auth (Owner only). Square Hosted Checkout for payments. Twilio for SMS.

**Entities:** MenuItem, Slot, Order, OrderItem, Settings.

Supabase anon key is public but RLS blocks unauthorized access. Service Role Key and Square/Twilio keys live only in Supabase Edge Function environment secrets. Raw customer phone never sent to browser except to authenticated Owner. Helper receives server-masked phone only. Totals, slot counts, and paid status are server-only.

**ADR list:** ADR-1 Supabase PostgreSQL + RLS. ADR-2 Edge Functions for all sensitive ops. ADR-3 Square Hosted Checkout. ADR-4 Server-side totals only. ADR-5 Atomic slot booking transaction. ADR-6 Lazy hold expiry. ADR-7 Phone in DB only, masked for Helper. ADR-8 PIN as bcrypt hash, never returned. ADR-9 Customer token = server-generated UUID. ADR-10 Supabase Auth for Owner only.

# SPEC.md

## One-liner
A booking, payment, messaging, and intake-form hub for a single massage studio: clients select a service, pay via Stripe, message the studio, and upload health intake forms — all in one place.

## Users & Roles

| Role | What they can do today | Must NEVER be able to do |
|---|---|---|
| **Client** | Book a service, pay via Stripe, read own bookings, send and receive messages with the studio, upload and view own intake files | Read another client's bookings, messages, or files · Create a booking record without a verified Stripe payment · Change their own or anyone else's role |
| **Staff** | Identical to client in current code — no additional permissions exist | Read any client's bookings, messages, or files unless explicitly assigned · Change any user's role · Process refunds or alter booking status |
| **Admin** | Identical to client in current code — no elevated permissions exist | Be billed for a service · Have their data mixed in with client data · Be blocked from viewing all bookings and messages (they *should* have full read access — currently they do not) |

---

## Core Loop

1. Client signs up or signs in → Supabase Auth issues a JWT (a short-lived signed ticket that proves who you are).
2. Client views the public service list → reads the `services` table.
3. Client clicks **"Book and pay"** → browser sends only the `serviceId` to the `checkout` Edge Function (a small piece of server code that runs in the cloud).
4. Edge Function looks up the price in the database, creates a Stripe Checkout session (a hosted payment page), and returns a URL.
5. Client completes payment on Stripe's hosted page.
6. Stripe sends a signed "payment done" message (webhook) to the `stripe-webhook` Edge Function.
7. The function verifies the signature and writes a `paid` booking row using the admin database key (bypassing client-level restrictions — this is intentional and correct).
8. Client can now send messages to the studio and upload their intake form.

---

## Features (with testable acceptance criteria)

### F1 — Public Service Listing
- Any visitor, logged in or not, can fetch service names and prices from the `services` table.

### F2 — Stripe Checkout
- Clicking "Book and pay" calls `checkout` with only the `serviceId`.
- Unauthenticated requests receive HTTP 401.
- The amount charged by Stripe equals `price_cents` from the database — not any value from the browser.
- A Stripe-hosted URL is returned; the browser redirects to it.
- A non-existent `serviceId` receives HTTP 404.

### F3 — Booking Creation via Webhook
- A `bookings` row with `status = 'paid'` is created only after Stripe's HMAC (cryptographic) signature is verified successfully.
- A request with a bad or missing signature returns HTTP 400.
- Replaying the same Stripe event (Stripe retries on network failures) does not create a duplicate booking (`onConflict: 'stripe_session'`).

### F4 — Messaging
- A user can insert a message only when `from_id = auth.uid()` (enforced by a database policy, not the browser).
- A user can read only messages where they are the sender or the recipient.
- Messages over 2,000 characters are rejected by the database.
- Message text is rendered with React's automatic character escaping — no raw HTML injection is possible.

### F5 — File Upload (Intake Forms)
- Only PDF, PNG, or JPG files under 5 MB are accepted.
- Files are stored under `{userId}/` in a private storage bucket.
- A user can write only to their own folder (enforced by a database storage policy).

### F6 — File Viewing
- Opening a file generates a time-limited (60-second) signed URL — a temporary link that expires automatically.
- A user can generate signed URLs only for files in their own folder (enforced by storage policy).

# SPEC.md

## One-liner
A web booking site for a massage studio where authenticated clients browse services, pay online via Stripe, upload health intake forms, and message the studio.

## Users & Roles

| Role | What the code currently lets them do | Must NEVER be able to do |
|------|--------------------------------------|--------------------------|
| **Unauthenticated visitor** | Read the public service list (names + prices) | Book, pay, view bookings, message, upload or view any files |
| **Client** (authenticated) | Book any listed service and pay; view own bookings; upload intake forms to own private folder; open own files via 60-second signed links; send and receive messages | See another client's bookings, files, or messages; edit their own role; change any service price; write a booking record directly (only the webhook may) |
| **Staff** | **Currently identical to client at the database layer** — no elevated policies exist | Change service prices or names; change any user's role; read any client's intake forms or full message history without an explicit database policy granting that |
| **Admin** | **Currently identical to client at the database layer** — management requires the Supabase dashboard directly | Let any role be self-assigned; expose one client's health data to another person; block a client's right to delete their own data |

> **Important:** The `user_roles` table stores the three role values, but **no Row Level Security (RLS — database rules controlling which rows each user may touch) policy grants staff or admin any permissions beyond a regular client.** The `role` column is recorded but never consulted by any database rule.

## Core Loop

1. Visitor signs up or logs in → Supabase Auth issues a **JWT** (JSON Web Token — a tamper-proof login ticket the browser carries on every request).
2. Visitor views the public service list (no login required).
3. Authenticated client clicks "Book and pay" → browser sends their JWT and a `serviceId` to the `checkout` **Edge Function** (a small program that runs on Supabase's servers, not in the browser).
4. Edge Function verifies the JWT, looks up `price_cents` from the database (the browser never decides the price), and creates a Stripe Checkout session.
5. Browser is redirected to Stripe's hosted payment page (card data never touches this app).
6. After successful payment, Stripe sends a cryptographically signed event to the `stripe-webhook` Edge Function.
7. Webhook verifies the signature, then writes a `paid` booking record using the **service-role key** (a special credential that bypasses RLS — used only server-side).
8. Client uploads intake forms to their private storage folder.
9. Client and studio exchange messages.

## Features that exist — with testable acceptance criteria

| # | Feature | How to verify it works |
|---|---------|----------------------|
| 1 | **Public service list** | An unauthenticated HTTP `GET /rest/v1/services` returns rows containing `id`, `name`, `price_cents`. |
| 2 | **Stripe checkout** | An authenticated client calls `checkout` with a valid `serviceId`; the response contains a `url` starting with `https://checkout.stripe.com`; the `unit_amount` in the resulting Stripe session equals the `price_cents` stored in the database — not a value the browser supplied. |
| 3 | **Idempotent booking on payment** | After `checkout.session.completed` fires once, exactly one row exists in `bookings` with `status = 'paid'`. Replaying the same webhook event does not create a second row (the **upsert** — "insert if new, update if exists" — on the unique `stripe_session` column handles this). |
| 4 | **Private file upload** | An authenticated client can upload a PDF, PNG, or JPEG ≤ 5 MB to `client-files/<their-uid>/`. Attempting to read that path as a different authenticated user returns an error. |
| 5 | **Signed file access** | `openFile` produces a URL that works for 60 seconds; that same URL returns an error after 60 seconds. |
| 6 | **Messaging** | An authenticated user can insert a message only when `from_id = auth.uid()`. Both `from_id` and `to_id` users can read the message; a third user cannot. |
| 7 | **Role protection** | An authenticated client attempting to `INSERT` or `UPDATE` their own `user_roles` row via the anon key receives an error. |

## Known Risks

1. Admin and staff roles exist in the database but grant zero extra permissions; all management requires the Supabase dashboard.
2. File MIME types (the label that says what kind of file something is) are validated only in the browser; the storage policy does not re-check content type on the server.
3. A client can address a message to any `user_id`, including other clients, with no restriction.
4. `sender_name` is free text; a user can write any name and it will appear in the recipient's message list without challenge.
5. No rate limiting is visible on Edge Functions or the messages insert policy.
6. No explicit **CORS** (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — a browser rule controlling which websites may call an API) configuration on Edge Functions; behavior depends on Supabase platform defaults.
7. No audit trail exists for file access, signed-URL generation, message reads, or admin dashboard actions.

## In Plain English

- **The browser holds no payment secrets.** The Stripe API key lives only inside Supabase Edge Functions; the browser receives only a redirect URL to Stripe's own page.
- **Row Level Security is the real lock on the database.** Every table has rules saying "only touch your own rows." The publicly visible anon key can only do what those rules allow — if a rule has a gap, data could be exposed.
- **The booking record is written by Stripe, not the browser.** Stripe sends a cryptographically signed event; the webhook verifies the signature before writing anything. A client cannot fake a paid booking.
- **Files are private, but only the uploader can access them through the app.** Even the admin cannot read client intake forms via the application today.
- **Health forms live on a third-party cloud server.** Clients upload files containing medical history to Supabase's servers. Privacy law may impose obligations on how that data is stored, accessed, and retained.
